🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Torch 1.13 adds a new feature: Inlined prim::PythonOp for Autograd Function Export (#74765). When tracing, all operations in the autograd function will be recorded as a subgraph of autograd function node. However, this subgraph seems to be useless if a custom symbolic function is implemented in autograd function defination or registered by register_custom_symbolic_op, in which cases the autograd function will be exported as one single node.
In my cases, some operations in my custom autograd functions may also be incompatible with this subgraph process or the following passes. Is it possible that a parameter is added in torch.onnx.export interface to control this subgraph trace or just skip subgraph tracing when a symbolic function is registered by register_custom_op_symbolic or implemented in the autograd function defination?

import torch

class MyRelu(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod

🐛 Describe the bug
With pre-built PyTorch > 1.11, I have issues with variable length sequences with a JIT-traced model on T4 devices.
The following chart shows the latency of running forward on a JIT model with batches of varying lengths. Batches are sorted longest first, so we should expect a (mostly) monotonously-decreasing function.
With PyTorch 1.11.0, we see the monotonously-decreasing function, with trivial exceptions, on both a T4 and a V100 (yellow and orange series). It's expected that the T4 is ~3x slower than the V100 for this model.
With PyTorch 1.13, the V100 is roughly as fast as 1.11, but with notable exceptions to the monotonously-decreasing function (dark blue series).
With PyTorch 1.13 and a T4, we can interpolate two wildly different curves (gray series).
The only setting that seems to fix it somewhat is torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False (light blue series). But this is not a sufficient solution for the intended use-case. I've tried most of the settings that come up in similar issues, with no effect.

🐛 Describe the bug
Hello, an unexpected behaviour appeared in PyTorch 1.13.0. I do not see it in Release Notes. Or is it a feature? Why can't I do it this way?
The following code works well in 1.12.1 but fails in 1.13.0:
import torch

mask = torch.full((3,), True, dtype=bool, device='cuda')
array = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3], dtype=torch.float32, device='cpu')
array = array[mask]
print(array)

class CFlow(torch.nn.Module):

        self.decoders = [load_decoder_arch(c, pool_dim) for pool_dim in self.pool_dims]
        self.decoders = [decoder.to(c.device) for decoder in self.decoders]
        params = list(self.decoders[0].parameters())
        for l in range(1, L):
            params += list(self.decoders[l].parameters())
        # optimizer
        self.optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=c.lr)
        self.N=256

    def forward(self, x):
        P = c.condition_vec
        #print(self.decoders)
        self.decoders = [decoder.eval() for decoder in self.decoders]
        height = list()
        width = list()

        test_loss = 0.0
        test_count = 0
        start = time.time()

        with torch.no_grad():
            for l, layer in enumerate(self.pool_layers):
                e = activation[layer]  # BxCxHxW

                S = H * W
                E = B * S
                #

                    width.append(W)
                #

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
The L1 regularization, a.k.a Lasso, is an important regularization term in machine learning.
However, PyTorch currently implements only L2 weight decay in the optimizer class.
This is unfortunate as an efficient implementation of L1 regularization requires using the sign of the gradients for regularization.
Although an implementation is available in TorchLayers, this implementation does not have the generality of PyTorch Optimizer parameter groups. Also, using hooks to use the gradients during backward exposes users to the limitations of hooks when using other PyTorch tools such as TorchDynamo.
The best solution would be to add a new parameter to the _Optimizer base class, which could calculate L1 weight decay with a similar mechanism as how it currently calculates L2 weight decay.
As this is already available in TensorFlow/Keras, I think that this will be very useful for the wider PyTorch community.
Alternatives
I have implemented my own custom hooks due to the limitations in the TorchLayers implementation such as not being able to specify parameter groups.
However, in all cases, users must implement their own hooks, which is time-consuming and bug-prone.
Considering the importance of lasso regularization, I do not think that its inclusion in the base optimizer would be problematic.
Additional context
Perhaps the new variable could be named lasso_decay since weight_decay has already been taken by L2 regularization.
cc @vincentqb @jbschlosser @albanD @janeyx99

🐛 Describe the bug
I haven't looked too deep into this, but here's an explanation.
UPD: Root cause: _print_Pow doesn't handle negative exponents. Example: 1/foo will be handled by _print_Pow and [foo] * -1 is [].
We have a custom pretty-printer for C++ and Triton code that's used in codegen (see texpr and cexpr below).
Something is broken in one of the classes (CppPrinter, TritonPrinter, ExprPrinter), which throws out part of the expression.
The output below compares to the default printer that comes with SymPy. More on printing:
https://docs.sympy.org/latest/modules/printing.html?highlight=doprint#printing
Also: there's likely another bug(?): I'm not sure why TritonPrinter and CppPrinter use different division (/ vs //).
Repro:
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import sympy
from torch._inductor.codegen.triton import texpr
from torch._inductor.codegen.cpp import cexpr

s1 = sympy.Symbol('foo', integer=True)
expr = s1/(2.0*s1 - 1) - 1/(2.0*s1 - 1)

print(type(expr))
# sympy.core.add.Add

# Default pprinter:
print(str(expr))
# 'foo/(2.0*foo - 1) - 1/(2.0*foo - 1)'

# Triton
print(texpr(expr))
# '((-1)*) + (foo*)'

# CPP (uses ExprPrinter as texpr)
print(cexpr(expr))
#  '((-1)*) + (foo*)'

🐛 Describe the bug
When evaluating large models on different machines, my co-developers and I noticed the produced results were different despite doing all we can for reproducibility (setting seeds, setting torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True etc.)
The differences between machines appear only when using CUDA tensors, i.e., when keeping everything on CPU, which is very slow, all machines produce the same output.
After some bug testing, we found the culprit to be torch.multinomial , which we use to sample from an output distribution. When checking the random state before and after sampling, we notice that it advances differently between machines when using CUDA tensors, but advances the same when using CPU.
We were able to get a minimal code sample to produce the same effect:
CPU example:
import torch

torch.manual_seed(1234)
torch.cuda.manual_seed(1234)

t = torch.rand(256, 100000)
s1 = torch.get_rng_state()
_ = torch.multinomial(t, 1)
s2 = torch.get_rng_state()

sum(s2-s1)
This leads to the same RNG advance on different machines tensor(128, dtype=torch.uint8) .
CUDA example:
import torch

torch.manual_seed(1234)
torch.cuda.manual_seed(1234)

t = torch.rand(256, 100000).to("cuda")
s1 = torch.cuda.get_rng_state()
_ = torch.multinomial(t, 1)
s2 = torch.cuda.get_rng_state()

sum(s2-s1)
This leads to different RNG advances on different machines tensor(113, dtype=torch.uint8) vs tensor(160, dtype=torch.uint8) .
We were able to determine that it has to do with GPU memory size/full tensor size, i.e., when limiting the tensor shape to anything from [1, 50000] to [5, 50000], all machines advance the CUDA RNG by the same amount (4) for each call of torch.multinomial.
However, beyond this the first machine (with smaller GPU) advances the RNG by 8, while the machine with bigger GPU keeps steps of 4 until a size of [13, 50000].
This means that despite all test machines being able to fit the network on their GPUs and perform inference with the same batch size, and us taking steps to ensure reproducibility, we still cannot reproduce results reliably without switching to CPU ( torch.multinomial(t.to("cpu"), 1).to("cuda") ).
Is this a known issue? Is there a way around this behaviour that does not require falling back to slow CPU-based sampling?

Bigger GPU:

Here is a simple test script:

x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.empty(1, device="cuda"))
params_groups = [{
    "params": [x],

}]

🐛 Describe the bug
torch.pow(x, y) has incorrect backward result when the base (x)  is real negative and exponent(y) is complex.
Because the backward propagation to the y uses log(x) in its computation. But when x is real and negative, the result is nan. But in the case that any one in x and y is complex, the pow should be considered a complex function.
pow(x, y) = exp(log(x) * y)

dpow(x, y) / dx = y * pow(x, y - 1)
dpow(x, y) / dy = pow(x, y) * log(x)

According to torch's convention of complex gradient. the backward of x and y are

  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp
    
    
        Lines 441 to 459
      in
      4cb6bbb
    
  
  
    

        
          
           Tensor pow_backward_exponent( 
        

        
          
               Tensor grad, 
        

        
          
               const Tensor& self, 
        

        
          
               const Tensor& exponent, 
        

        
          
               Tensor result) { 
        

        
          
             Tensor cond; 
        

        
          
             if (exponent.is_complex()) { 
        

        
          
               auto is_real_exp = 
        

        
          
                   at::logical_and(at::imag(exponent) == 0, at::real(exponent) >= 0); 
        

        
          
               cond = at::logical_and(self == 0, is_real_exp); 
        

        
          
             } else { 
        

        
          
               cond = at::logical_and(self == 0, exponent >= 0); 
        

        
          
             } 
        

        
          
             auto out = 
        

        
          
                 grad * 
        

        
          
                 at::where( 
        

        
          
                     cond, at::zeros({}, grad.options()), (result * self.log()).conj()); 
        

        
          
             return handle_r_to_c(exponent, out); 
        

        
          
           } 
        
    
  


g_x = (grad.conj() * y * pow(x, y - 1)).conj()
g_y =  (grad.conj() * pow(x, y) * log(x)).conj()

respectively. but the log(x) should be considered function on complex plane. So I propose to fix it with the following change:
g_x = (grad.conj() * y * pow(x, y - 1)).conj()
g_y =  (grad.conj() * pow(x, y) * log(x.astype(y.dtype))).conj()

📚 The issue
I believe that example for any torch operator should be in such a way that it is obvious what to see what the operator does. This is more important for an operator that is as simple as torch.mode. The current example does not show the tensor and it is constructed in such a way that all the modes occur together.  So, the indices returned are all the same and leads to confusion (e.g. a post on StackOverflow).

>>> b = torch.randint(4, (5, 7))
>>> b
tensor([[0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 2],
        [0, 3, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1],
        [2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3],
        [2, 2, 3, 0, 1, 1, 0],

torch.return_types.mode(
values=tensor([0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]),

📚 The doc issue
The type requirement for real in torch.complex(real, imag, *, out=None) is float or double, so I used the wrong type to test in pytorch 1.12, and found that the thrown information describes the type of real requiring Half , Float or Double.
To sum up, I suggest adding half to the real type in the documentation to avoid misleading.
import torch
real = torch.rand([2], dtype=torch.float32)
imag = torch.randint(-8192, 32, [2], dtype=torch.int32)
out = torch.complex(real, imag)

result: RuntimeError: Expected both inputs to be Half, Float or Double tensors but got Float and Int
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
I suggest adding half to the real type in the documentation to avoid misleading.
